newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi mulls finance options for plane deal.
newsitem.headline: Saudi mulls finance options for plane deal.

text.p: Saudi Arabia was considering several options to finance part of its $6 billion order for U.S. commercial aircraft, including local and regional borrowing, a leading Saudi banker said on Wednesday.

Omar Bajammal, deputy manager of the National Commercial Bank, Saudi Arabia's largest commercial bank, said the bank was updating a 1995 proposal to the Saudi government and Saudi Arabian Airlines Corp on the financing.

He told Reuters by telephone from Jeddah that no decisions had been taken and that some of the options being considered were borrowing from Islamic financial institutions -- which forbid levying interest -- in Saudi Arabia and the Gulf region.

"There is serious work now to finalise the financing arrangements. There is nothing definite. There are several options including going to Islamic financial institutions locally and regionally," he said.
Bajammal ruled out press reports that Saudi Arabia would go to the international market for funding and said the government remained determined to avoid any such move.
Asked how much of the financing was being discussed, he said: "There is nothing definite. It depends on the needs."
The deal is for five 747s and 23 777s made by Boeing Co and 29 MD-90s and four freight MD-11s made by McDonnell Douglas Corp.
Saudi officials, industry executives and bankers had said the kingdom would finance the deal from its own resources.
Bankers said on Wednesday Saudi Arabia -- a major beneficiary of higher 1996 oil prices -- might want to use the extra oil revenue to eliminate its budget deficit and boost its foreign reserves.
"Money for the plane deal would take a large slice of their extra revenue. So they might think of borrowing a little bit for the planes," one banker said.
Economists speak of oil earnings exceeding the budgeted amount by between $6 and $10 billion this year.
Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil producer and exporter, had suffered cash flow problems for the past few years due to lower oil prices and the huge cost of the 1991 Gulf War.
Bankers now say the kingdom hoped to wipe out its 1996 budget deficit -- forecast at $4.9 billion on spending of $40 billion -- for the first time in more than 10 years.

The London-based Middle East Economic Digest (MEED) said in its October 4 issue that Saudi Arabia had "reversed its plan to finance the...aircraft order from internal resources and will seek up to half the funds from overseas. Part of the funding is expected to come from regional Islamic financiers."
It said Saudi Arabia had also "canvassed institutions in the U.S. and Japan about tax lease capacity".

Saudi Arabia's Defence and Aviation Minister Prince Sultan, who finalised the aircraft deal in Washington last October, told the London-based al-Hayat newspaper then that Saudi Arabia would receive the first of the 61 aircraft on order in 18 months and hoped to complete payment of the deal ahead of schedule.

In what appeared to be a relaxed payment schedule, he said: "We have agreed to pay $10 million only as a first instalment, then we pay $67 million for next year, 1996. As of 1997, and for seven years, we will pay the remaining instalments in phases."
Bankers in the kingdom said they believed some money has been paid for the aircraft, but did not have details.
